I started a diary for quasi intellectual reasons. Mainly to jot down any ideas that I have while wandering about or at work.

Today one of those thoughts was about why I love handwritting ideas into a book and came to the conclusion that it is a private thought captured in that moment in all its imperfections. Like a photograph of where my mind was at that moment in time. That it is there and only there, no where less.

Contrary to the internet where everything is memed and passed on; forever imprinted and collected in databases. Sold on to governments and advertising companies to control and influence us into the way they think.

I sat there scribbling into my diary these half hashed out concepts when my thoughts turned to Winston from 1984 and his diary. The reasons he started writing in his diary and got an orwellian shiver down my spine.

That I could see this diary as an act of private rebellion made me feel rather embarrassed like a teenager trying to rebel against their parents.

I want to know what your opinions are on this and whether you keep a diary or have a private act of meaningless rebellion.

Orwellian Realisation: How many of you have diaries?

I was given my first diary at age 10. At first I was an intermittent diarist. Since my teenage years I have been more regular in my diary habits. I now keep a complex of diaries that has developed over the years. Roughly, I maintain the following:

  • engagement diaries, indicating appointments and other time-bound tasks (these are supported by a monthly summary sheet that I keep on my desk under a pane of glass for quick reference)
  • a daily record sheet (pre-printed since 1991, so I just fill in the blanks), recording my clothes, calorie intake, weight, cash and card expenditures, bank balance, resting blood pressure, heart rate, bedtime, time I got up, location during the day, drugs taken (both licit and otherwise), and number of people I had sex with
  • a personal written diary (now actually recorded on my phone, earlier on an HP-200LX, and before that on paper), in which I from time to time, though not daily, record my thoughts, feelings, hopes, ambitions, and notes about how irritating the people sitting next to me on the tube are for (a) not bathing, and (b) attempting to read my diary
  • a daily to-do list, which records tasks I set for myself, along with timings, completion mark, and weekly summaries of my average performance

All of these are supplemented by a large network of files and folders containing relevant data on my personal life (records of personal conversations, birthdays and phone numbers to remember, back copies of Christmas card and Christmas present lists (given and received), archived e-mails, and all the other stuff that it's useful to maintain), records of my obligations (I retain copies of all bills, though I am in the process of converting these to purely electronic format), notes on books and papers I have read or wish to read, or have written or intend to write, photographs, recordings, and so on. Oh, and gym records and an index of my general fitness.

At one stage many of these were maintained in "filofax" format, but some years ago I decided that the costs of filofax paper and files were too great, and I switched to A5 format. I now mix this with a very simple electronic format.

And, since you are probably wondering, all of this can be maintained in about 20 minutes a day, plus occasional jottings in my "to do" book.

Edit: I suppose I might be said to have been a "life logger" avant la lettre.
